topic_ko: 냄새에 잘 반응하지만 말로 표현하는 데는 서툴다
_note: 유형별 묶음 구조. 같은 33번 지문이라도 유형마다 passage를 다르게 paraphrase 한다. order/insert/irrelevant/writing 은 구조상 예외.

passage: Describing what something smells like is the most basic way to talk about our sense of smell, yet even this turns out to be hard.
English offers no words that capture smells the way "blue" or "green" capture colors.
Instead, we describe a smell by naming its source, calling things "flowery," "fruity," or "fishy."
Even familiar odors are hard to identify once they are taken out of their usual setting.
In one study, most people could not name very common smells such as beer, roses, or motor oil.
Yet anyone would happily drink the beer while refusing the motor oil, which shows that we react to smells correctly.
Evolution has shaped our brain so that we respond well to odors through action but are poorly equipped to put them into words.
choices: that we respond to smells correctly yet struggle to describe them in words
why some smells are far more pleasant than others to most people
how English speakers invented special vocabulary just for odors
why familiar smells become stronger when removed from their context
how evolution gave humans a sharper sense of smell than other animals
theme.explanation_ko: 우리는 냄새에 행동으로는 정확히 반응하지만, 영어에는 냄새 자체를 가리키는 단어가 없어 말로 표현하는 데는 서툴다는 내용. ①이 주제로 정답.
theme.distractor_ko: ②냄새의 호불호 비교, ③냄새 전용 어휘 발명, ④맥락 밖 냄새의 강화, ⑤후각의 우월성은 본문 초점이 아니다.

passage: We should recognize a curious gap in how we deal with smells.
English simply lacks words that name a smell itself the way color words name colors.
To talk about an odor, we fall back on its source, saying something smells "flowery" or "fishy."
Even common smells become hard to name once they leave their familiar setting.
In one experiment most people failed to identify beer, roses, or motor oil by smell alone.
Still, those same people would drink the beer and avoid the motor oil without hesitation.
So we should accept that our brains respond to odors accurately through action, even though we are clumsy at describing them.
choices: 후각을 키우려면 다양한 냄새를 자주 맡아 보아야 한다.
색을 가리키는 단어처럼 냄새 전용 단어를 새로 만들어야 한다.
냄새에 행동으로는 정확히 반응하지만 말로 표현하는 능력은 부족함을 인정해야 한다.
위험한 냄새는 반드시 경고 라벨로 표시해야 한다.
익숙한 냄새일수록 더 쉽게 이름을 댈 수 있다.

claim.distractor_ko: ①후각 훈련, ②냄새 단어 발명, ④경고 라벨, ⑤익숙함과 명명 용이성은 핵심 주장이 아니다.

passage: Saying what something smells like is the simplest way to talk about smell, and even that is surprisingly difficult.
Our language has no smell words to match color words like "blue" or "green."
So we borrow the source of the odor, calling things "fruity" or "fishy."
Familiar odors slip away from us when they appear outside their usual context.
In a study, most participants could not name beer, roses, or motor oil by smell.
Yet they would still drink the beer and reject the motor oil, reacting correctly all the same.
Our brains, shaped by evolution, handle odors well in action but poorly in words.

passage: Talking about a smell is the most basic part of describing our sense of smell, and yet it is oddly hard to do.
There are no English words for smells the way "blue" and "green" exist for colors.
Instead we point to the source, labeling things "flowery," "fruity," or "fishy."
Take an odor out of its usual context and even a familiar one becomes hard to name.
In one study most people could not name beer, roses, or motor oil from smell alone.
Still, no one would confuse the two: they would drink the beer and shun the motor oil.
Evolution left us able to act on odors correctly but unable to speak about them easily.
